title: Synchronous Nodular Epithelial Hyperplasia and Type A Microthymoma Adjacent to a Thymic Cyst: A Report of a Rare Case.
authors: Bunno Y, Yamamoto M, Miyazaki R et al.
abstract: Thymic cysts are uncommon benign lesions of the anterior mediastinum and are frequently detected incidentally on imaging studies. Microscopic thymoma and microthymoma are extremely rare microscopic thymic epithelial proliferations that are usually identified only by histopathological examination. Their relationship to thymic cysts and to each other remains poorly understood. A 54-year-old woman was referred to our institution after an anterior mediastinal lesion was incidentally detected on routine chest computed tomography (CT). Magnetic resonance imaging and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/CT findings were consistent with a thymic cyst. Robot-assisted thoracoscopic resection of the cyst with the adjacent thymic tissue was performed for definitive diagnosis and treatment. Histopathological examination revealed a unilocular thymic cyst accompanied by two incidental microscopic thymic epithelial lesions within the adjacent thymic tissue: a 0.6-mm microscopic thymoma and a 2.0-mm Type A microthymoma. Based on their characteristic size and histological features, both lesions were diagnosed without additional immunohistochemical analysis. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient remains free of recurrence 18 months after surgery. To our knowledge, the coexistence of microscopic thymoma and Type A microthymoma adjacent to a thymic cyst is exceptionally rare. The close proximity and similar histological features of these lesions suggest that they may represent different stages within a continuous morphological spectrum of microscopic thymic epithelial proliferations rather than entirely distinct entities. Furthermore, this case highlights the potential value of careful pathological examination of thymic tissue adjacent to resected thymic cysts for detecting occult microscopic epithelial lesions and improving pathological assessment.

title: Atypical Type A Thymoma Identified in Slowly Growing Pulmonary Metastases from Type A Thymoma: A Case Report.
authors: Shintani H, Wakama S, Tokuhara K et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Type A thymoma is generally considered a low-risk thymoma subtype with an excellent prognosis and low rates of distant metastasis. Atypical type A thymoma is a recently established entity characterized by more aggressive biological behavior despite retaining the morphology of conventional type A thymoma. Patients with primary conventional type A thymoma who subsequently develop recurrence with atypical histological features are extremely rare.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 79-year-old man was referred to our hospital due to gradual enlargement of bilateral pulmonary nodules. Seven years earlier, he had undergone complete resection of an anterior mediastinal tumor, which had been diagnosed as conventional type A thymoma. Retrospective review of preoperative computed tomography images revealed that small pulmonary nodules had already been present at the time of the initial surgery but had yet to be identified. The nodules enlarged slowly from 3 mm to 10 mm and from 3 mm to 7 mm over the 7-year period. Positron emission tomography showed no abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake. After thoracoscopic wedge resection of the left lower lobe lesion, histopathological examination demonstrated pulmonary metastasis of type A thymoma with focal hypercellularity and increased mitotic activity, consistent with atypical type A thymoma. No necrosis was identified. The Ki-67 labeling indices of the primary and metastatic lesions were 7% and 20%, respectively.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates that even apparently low-risk type A thymoma may exhibit indolent but metastatic behavior and may develop atypical histological features during a prolonged clinical course. Careful long-term surveillance and detailed pathological evaluation, including assessment of the Ki-67 labeling index, may be important in patients with type A thymoma.

title: Learning Curve in Thoracoscopic Mediastinal Mass Excision: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study Using Cumulative Sum and Multivariable Regression Analysis.
authors: Elsayed K, Ibrahim GK, Elghanam M et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) mediastinal mass excision has become the standard approach for anterior mediastinal lesions. Understanding its learning curve is essential for surgical training and quality assurance. The primary objective was to quantify the association between cumulative case experience (case sequence number) and operative time, the primary outcome, using cumulative sum (CUSUM) analysis and multivariable regression modelling. We tested the null hypothesis that operative time does not change with increasing case sequence after adjustment for patient-, tumour- and country-related factors. Secondary objectives were to estimate the number of cases required to achieve proficiency and to compare perioperative outcomes across learning phases and between participating countries.
METHODS: This multicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted at five academic and tertiary-care centers in Egypt and Saudi Arabia between January 2023 and December 2025. Seventy-seven consecutive patients undergoing VATS excision of mediastinal masses were categorized into three phases: Early (first 20 cases), Intermediate (next 20 cases), and Late (last 37 cases). Cumulative sum (CUSUM) analysis was performed. Operative outcomes, including operative time, blood loss, conversion rate, and postoperative complications, were compared across phases and between countries (Egypt vs. Saudi Arabia). Multivariable linear regression and a linear mixed-effects model with participating centre as a random intercept were used to identify factors independently associated with operative time.
RESULTS: Mean operative time significantly decreased across phases (189.5 ± 21.9 vs. 156.5 ± 26.4 vs. 139.7 ± 30.5 minutes; p < 0.001). CUSUM analysis demonstrated a learning curve inflection point between cases 20 and 26. After adjustment for age, sex, body mass index, myasthenia gravis, presence of a discrete mass, thymic neoplasm and country, case sequence number remained independently associated with shorter operative time (β = -1.14 min per case; 95% CI -1.47 to -0.80; p < 0.001; R² = 0.48, adjusted R² = 0.42), with consistent estimates using robust standard errors and a mixed-effects model with centre as a random intercept (β = -1.37; 95% CI -1.80 to -0.95). Patients treated in Saudi Arabia (n = 7) were older and more often had discrete neoplastic masses, but operative time did not differ significantly between countries before (p = 0.128) or after adjustment (p = 0.548). Conversion to open surgery occurred in 3.9% (n = 3), all in the Intermediate and Late phases. Overall mortality was 2.6% (n = 2), both in the Late phase and associated with complex cases. No significant differences were observed regarding ICU stay, hospital stay, or postoperative complications.
CONCLUSION: VATS mediastinal mass excision is safe and feasible, with surgical proficiency achieved after approximately 20-26 cases. Operative time was the most reliable indicator of learning progression, and the learning effect persisted after multivariable adjustment for patient-, tumour- and country-related factors. Structured mentorship and careful case selection are recommended during the early learning phase.
